news.title: Once a Blue: Ron Harris
news.body_en: To mark the 82nd birthday of our record appearance maker Ron Harris, we revisit an interview he conducted reflecting on his illustrious Chelsea career. ‘Chopper’ Harris made his Blues debut in 1962 and his final appearance in 1980, 795 games and 14 goals later. He was the captain that lifted our first FA Cup trophy and first piece of European silverware, in the form of the Cup Winners’ Cup. Chopper’s Chelsea journey was quite a ride, so buckle up and enjoy this Q&A… Can you remember your first appearance way back in 1962? I captained the England youth side on the Wednesday and we won some little World Cup, and Tommy Docherty was there with my parents. He told me I'd be in the first team on the Saturday for the game against Sheffield Wednesday. We won 1-0 with Mickey Harrison getting the goal, and I marked a lad called Johnny Fantham. It was a real thrill for me as a 17-year-old lad. You had to bide your time before getting a proper run in the team, didn't you? I did stay in the team for a few games, but we went up to Everton and got hammered. That was it for me until the next year; we got relegated and in the Second Division I got a chance later in the season and we ended up getting promoted. The last game was against Portsmouth and we had to win to go up. I think the final score was 7-0! After that, I think I was a regular until my old team-mate Eddie McCreadie took over as manager. He was very superstitious and I was sub just about every week, occasionally coming on if someone was injured. I think I set a Chelsea record of playing in two games in one day. He thought I could do with a run-out with the reserves, so I went and played for them, and then they got a taxi to pick me up from Stamford Bridge to take me to Millwall. We were 3-0 down and at half-time Jock Finnieston had to come off so I played the second half. I can't imagine too many have done that – and I went to training the next day! Clear something up for us – were you a full-back or a centre-half? Because I wasn't gifted with pace, I enjoyed playing alongside the centre-half. I wasn't a big, dominant fella – I'm 5ft 8in – but you learned how to cope in other ways, using your body in the right way to compete against bigger players. I don't know the exact statistics but I think I played just as many games as a full-back as I did as a central defender. When I first came into the side I just man-marked people: Besty, Greavsie, Denis Law. Wherever they went, I used to follow. If I never touched the ball in a game and they didn't either, I knew I'd done a good job. I have to say, the hardest to man-mark was George Best – well, he was the hardest to try and kick! For a fella who was frail and skinny, he wasn't a coward. He could hold his own against anybody. Right foot, left foot; inside or out, he could take you wherever he wanted. I played against Pele a couple of times, too, but I think Best was the best I ever came across. I don't know, but we all got on very well. There was always a players' lounge and it was only for the players and their wives and girlfriends. There was no animosity if you'd given someone a hard time on the pitch – once the final whistle was blown, everything was forgotten. What I can say is that I'd love to have played with Besty, he gave me a few chasings. Having spent the best part of two decades in the first team, I imagine it must be pretty hard for you to highlight your favourite games for the club... Bearing in mind I didn't score too many during my career, we took on the Hammers just before the 1966 World Cup at Stamford Bridge and I scored two fantastic goals. I sliced one past Peter Bonetti for an own goal and then I went up the other end and hit a fantastic volley past Jim Standen! So that's one game. Then, in the 1971 Cup Winners' Cup run, me and Ossie didn't play in the first leg against Club Brugge when we lost 2-0, but we came back for the return and won 4-0. They were a useful side so that was a memorable game. Obviously the replay against Leeds United in the 1970 FA Cup final is another that stands out more than most, when we beat a tremendous side and became the first Chelsea team to lift the FA Cup. Then there's the European Cup Winners' Cup in Athens – another replay! We lost a goal in the last few seconds of the final, which was played on the Wednesday, and then on the Friday we had a replay and won 2-1. You've picked quite a few cup games there. I guess it sums up Chelsea during your time there, doesn't it? I've always said we were so inconsistent in the league – we could beat anybody on our day, but often when it came to taking on the lesser sides we'd go and get beaten. But with the cup games, the bigger the crowd, the better our star men responded. We had a great team. Peter Bonetti was fantastic in goal and the back four didn't take any prisoners; John Hollins did a great job in midfield while Charlie Cooke and Huddy pulled the strings, and Peter Houseman was a workaholic on the wing; and then you've got Hutch, who was a perfect foil for Ossie. I have to say, Os was the one of the best players I ever played alongside. He was tough as well as incredibly skilful. We had such a camaraderie. If one of the lads was getting a bit of a rough time on the pitch then there'd be one of their mates to help them out. I was privileged to captain a bunch of great lads and tremendous players. The closest you came to winning the league was in the 1964/65 season, when the Blues were top with three games left to play. Was that the year of the Blackpool incident? I've spoken to Tom [Docherty] on many occasions and I think he'll tell you that's the one thing he regretted. We had games against Burnley and Blackpool coming up so we went up there to stay for a few days. Tom said, “You've got to be in at a certain time” and everyone came back, but then some of them snuck out through the fire escape. He ended up sending them home, bringing in a load of youngsters, and we got beaten 6-2 against Burnley. I scored in that game, but I'd have preferred the win. Anyway, that put paid to our chances. The atmosphere between the lads and Tom was off – the whole situation got blown out of proportion and upset the apple cart. If he'd have just fined them a week's wages then I think we'd have probably gone on to win the league. Is that a regret from your time at Chelsea? Not a regret, but it would have been nice. It was the closest we ever came to the title. The balance of the side was the bigger the game, the better they performed. I'm not being disrespectful to some of the less fashionable sides in the First Division, but we just didn't perform against them on the smaller stage. You mention how long you spent at the club, but did you ever consider leaving before finally moving on for Brentford in 1980? I remember captaining England Under-23s when Bill Nicholson was manager and he asked me if I'd be interested in going to the Spurs because they'd love to have me there. But I had absolutely no intention of going there, and they ended up buying Dave Mackay – that was the end of it. Then, when Danny Blanchflower took over as manager we got beaten badly up at Middlesbrough in his first game and things hadn't been going great before that. Danny said to me, “Look, I'll put you in the picture: I'm going with the younger lads. Would you be interested in going to Luton?” David Pleat was the manager at the time and he was someone I'd played alongside at England youth level. Pleaty came round to my house in Epsom for a chat. He told me that I only had to come in to training on a Monday and a Friday – he just needed a bit of an old head for all the youngsters in his squad, someone to look after them. I had two young kids myself at that time and didn't really want to be travelling up there twice a week so I turned them down. Your older brother Allan also played for Chelsea. Does he ever get fed up with being known as Chopper's brother?! I don't think so. In fact, I reckon most people probably remember him for his managerial partnership with Terry Venables at Spurs and Barcelona. He played over 100 games for Chelsea and had the one thing I never did – pace. Was he one of the reasons you joined Chelsea? Yeah. In my day you'd go around all of the clubs so I tried out West Ham, Arsenal, Spurs and others. Then Allan decided on Chelsea and I followed him. When he went there I was a ballboy until I left school. Then I signed for the club. The rest is history – 795 games, 13 or 14 goals depending on you speak to. I'll take the 14, don't worry about that! You almost became a cricketer for Middlesex. What happened? Maybe I'd have done both if the seasons didn't overlap. Ron Tindall always used to miss the start of the football because of the cricket. So I went to see Ted Drake at Chelsea and he offered me £7 per week and a rail pass for the year. I went up to Lord's and was offered £4 per week to join the groundstaff but I had to pay my expenses. I was from a working-class family, so that swayed me. What does it mean to be our record appearance maker? I served under seven managers and what each of them got from me was 110 per cent effort in training and on the Saturday. I'm so proud of playing more games than any other player in the history of Chelsea Football Club and it's a record I don't think will ever be beaten. A version of this interview was first published in the official Chelsea matchday programme. You can buy past copies of the programme here.

news.title: OTD: Fulham 1-4 Chelsea | 13 November 2004
Internationals: Rogers on target, Gusto features for France
news.body_en: Morgan Rogers maintained his impressive form by scoring in England's Nations League victory over Croatia this evening, while Malo Gusto started for France against Italy. Rogers has enjoyed an impressive start at Stamford Bridge since following his summer signing from Aston Villa. He has already contributed to ten goals in blue and earned a call-up from Thomas Tuchel for the latest round of England fixtures. The first came tonight at Wembley and Rogers, deployed on the right of the Three Lions' attack, broke the deadlock in the 24th minute. The goal was a poacher's effort, as the 24-year-old produced an intelligent close-range finish after a knock-down from Jude Bellingham. ICE COLD ❄️Morgan Rogers puts the Three Lions in front in the 24th minute 🙌#England #ThreeLions pic.twitter.com/lMCf51fP7F In the second half, Croatia equalised just before the hour-mark through Petar Sucic after the hosts failed to deal with a corner. However, England quickly restored their lead, with Harry Kane converting from the penalty spot on the night he became the Three Lions' most-capped player. Rogers went on to complete the full 90 minutes as England claimed a victory that leaves them second in Group C, three points behind Spain, who they take on this weekend at the Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid. Meanwhile, in Group A, Malo Gusto started for France in their 3-1 defeat to Italy, for whom Marco Palestra was an unused substitute. Michael Olise opened the scoring for the visitors in the tenth minute, but that advantage was wiped out midway through the first half when Pio Esposito found the net. In the second period, Italy went ahead when Davide Frattesi struck, and Esposito extended an advantage the hosts did not relinquish. Gusto played 77 minutes of the game before being replaced by Sael Kumbedi. The other Group A fixture saw Belgium clinch a 2-1 away win over Turkiye. Blues midfielder Romeo Lavia missed the game due to suspension, while goalkeeper Mike Penders was an unused substitute. At youth level, Shim Mheuka scored twice as England Under-20s claimed a 6-1 win over their  Czech Republic counterparts. Mheuka, currently on loan at Celtic, started alongside fellow Blue Jesse Derry, who is spending the campaign at Sporting CP, and completed his brace before half-time as England established a commanding four-goal lead. The Young Lions added to the second period, during which Chelsea defender Tayo Subuloye was introduced from the substitutes' bench. England remain top of the UEFA Under-20 Elite League, having won their four matches. Portugal are fifth in the table after losing 1-0 to Italy. Blues winger Leo Cardoso was introduced as a late substitute, coming on in the 77th minute, but couldn't help his country rescue a point. And at Under-18 level, Isaac Badu featured in the closing stages as Portugal Under-18s clinched a 1-0 win over Norway Under-18s in friendly action.

news.title: Home Sweet Home: How the Chelsea Women players are settling in at Stamford Bridge
news.body_en: This weekend's clash with Manchester City will be our sixth Women's Super League game held at Stamford Bridge since we made it our new home. We sat down with four of our Blues to see how they are finding the move... Last season we played four league matches at the Bridge, against Arsenal, Manchester City, London City Lionesses and Manchester United. Now, having already turned out five times in SW6, it feels like an ideal time to check in with our players to see how their new home suits them. The opinions coming from inside the dressing room are unanimous: the move has been a resounding success. Whether it's a settled matchday routine, the atmosphere inside the stadium, or the feeling of butterflies when emerging from the tunnel, it's clear how our players are benefitting from their surroundings. We sat down with three players who remember what it was like to play at Kingsmeadow - Nathalie Bjorn, Kadeisha Buchanan and Erin Cuthbert - and one who has only known the Bridge, summer signing Melvine Malard. Here's what they had to say. 'The locker room is really nice. You're able to really activate and prepare for the game a lot better because there's more space. Obviously, the pitch is really nice and the atmosphere, too. 'The more fans we get, the merrier. A few times they really showed up for us. 'We want to keep that going because we definitely enjoy it when we walk out, and there are a lot of people there. It really boosts us up and gets that really good feeling going that today is going to be a really good game.' 'Stamford Bridge suits our style of play. It’s a bigger pitch, we love the locker room and it’s our home now – it’s our castle. We know it’s a transition process and will take time, but playing at a big stadium is what everyone wants to do. I think the fans really do enjoy it, the same as the players. 'The history of the stadium evokes a lot of feelings. Whether it’s against a top team or a lower team in the league, it still brings that extra fire in you. 'It’s just a feeling you have in your body. It’s a bit hard to explain, but like I said, with all the history and all the good games and the big games we played there before, being able to do that every weekend is a really nice feeling. 'You can hear our supporters throughout the game, which is really nice. They even celebrate if we do a great tackle, so having that support all the time, celebrating the small wins and getting that encouragement from the fans, is really amazing. And when we played Arsenal, for example, there were fireworks and the display in the stands – it was really cool. It creates a great atmosphere when they add those things. 'I would say: “Bring your friends, go to Bottomless at the Bridge, and then watch us play. Have a good time, and some drinks!”' 'It feels good to play at Stamford Bridge. I really love to enjoy playing in front of the fans. I'm a player who likes to celebrate a lot with the fans. In fact, I need to do it! When I score, I need to go over to the fans to make sure everyone has the same pleasure as we do when we play football. 'Everything's more familiar. Last season it maybe sometimes felt like we were playing an away game there, even though we weren't. 'When it’s your home, you've got your familiar settings, you know exactly where you're going, you know where you're eating pre-match, where you're getting treatment, where you're talking to the coaches, where you're doing the tactics. Everything is second nature. 'And on a matchday, the last thing you want as players is to think about anything other than your performance. So having taken all those variables out, I feel like everyone's settled and feels at home at the Bridge now. 'Hopefully the fans feel at home with our performances on the pitch, and their surroundings as well. We want to keep building our fanbase, keep growing, and give them the performances to match that.' Come and cheer on Chelsea Women in Saturday's huge game against Manchester City at the Bridge!

news.title: Malo Gusto joins the ranks of Chelsea’s French centurions
news.body_en: Shortly before heading off to represent his country this week, Malo Gusto made his 100th Premier League appearance for Chelsea, becoming the eighth French international to hit a century for the Blues in that competition. Gusto is currently away as part of Zinedine Zidane’s France squad. They are attempting to hold on to top spot in their UEFA Nations League group and seal qualification for the quarter-finals in their final two games, against Marco Palestra’s Italy tonight and Turkiye on Sunday. In his last game before meeting up with Les Bleus, Gusto came off the bench for Chelsea in our Premier League away fixture at Sunderland, making his 100th appearance for the club in that competition, and 144th in total since arriving from Lyon three years ago. The 23-year-old joins an illustrious list of Frenchmen to have reached a century of games for the club in the Premier League, but who are the other seven Blues to have hit that landmark? Anelka was slow out the blocks for Chelsea, but he more than made up for it in his first full season, in 2008/09. A tally of 19 goals earned him the Premier League Golden Boot award – just the second Frenchman to win it, after Thierry Henry. He netted exactly half of his Premier League goals for the Blues that season, although his intelligent link play was an understated factor during a successful era for the club. The cultured defender was one half of an all-French centre-back pairing with Marcel Desailly that enjoyed plenty of success for club and country. In addition to his defensive strength and quality on the ball, particularly when spraying passes out from the back, Leboeuf also got his share of goals from penalties and some spectacular long-rangers. Famously the holding midfield player who was so good they named his position after him. ‘The Makelele role’ became a common term for a defensive-midfielder in the Premier League, but no one seemed to do it quite as well as him. He was a vital cog in the make-up of two title-winning sides, someone who made the game that much easier for his team-mates. Just like Gusto, the left-winger joined us from Lyon, and did so as the reigning Ligue 1 Player of the Year. Malouda hit top form during our 2009/10 Double-winning season as a key source of both goals and assists. Better was to follow in front of goal the following campaign, as he netted 13 times in the Premier League to finish as our leading scorer. Two-time Champions League winner Desailly joined the Blues shortly before going on to lift the 1998 World Cup with France – alongside Leboeuf – on home soil, and it was not long before Chelsea fans found out just why he was known as The Rock. The defender was at his imposing best in our 2000 FA Cup triumph and during our maiden voyage in the Champions League. He was also the natural successor to Dennis Wise as skipper. Some Chelsea fans have not forgiven Gallas for departing the club for Arsenal as part of the deal which brought Ashley Cole to Stamford Bridge in the summer of 2006, but there is no doubting the key role he played in two title-winning sides. His stunning late winner against Tottenham Hotspur lives long in the memory and he was also part of the defence which set a Premier League low of only 15 goals conceded in 2004/05. Although a quiet character, there was nothing understated about Kante’s performances as we reclaimed our top-flight crown from his former club Leicester City in 2016/17. He was the dominant midfield player in the country and an obvious choice for numerous individual prizes that term. There was also arguably no-one as important as NG in our run to Champions League glory in Porto in 2021, as he was named Man of the Match in virtually every knockout game that season,

news.title: Meet the Constant Contact small businesses activating at CFCW matchday
news.body_en:
Chelsea FC Women and our principal partner, Constant Contact, are making the most of one of the biggest occasions of the WSL season to give small businesses the opportunity to be part of a matchday at Stamford Bridge. On Saturday, the top two in the league table go head to head when the Blues host Manchester City and three companies, Leo's Circus, Cheer London Allstarz and Popchoir, will be showcasing their work to supporters there for the game. All three female-founded businesses are Constant Contact customers. Constant Contact, CFCW’s training kit partner, is the AI-powered marketing partner for small businesses, nonprofits, franchises, multi-location brands and estate agents. In the lead-up to their matchday at the Bridge, the founders of the businesses visited Cobham to meet CFCW stars Erin Cuthbert, Aggie Beever-Jones and Melvine Malard. They were keen to help with the project, sharing in the ideas generated for how the business could be seen by more people this weekend. Fans at the game will now see those ideas come to life on Saturday. The three businesses involved this matchday all focus on driving participation among local London communities. Leo's Circus is a circus and aerial school, running camps for children. They will be located nearby Britannia Gate from 11am to 1pm, performing circus skills. Children will have the chance to win a golden ticket, and a place at one of their circus camps, by completing the plate-spinning challenge. View this post on Instagram            
Cheer London Allstarz is a grassroots cheer and tumbling club. Their young squad will have a routine incorporating the players' celebration poses. Look out for that by the East Stand entrance at 11am. Popchoir is an adult community choir which will be performing by Britannia Gate from 12.15pm to 1.15pm, with songs that inspire excitement for gameday including their version of Blue Is The Colour. news.title: Isaac Collinson signs professional contract
news.body_en: Chelsea Football Club is pleased to announce that Academy goalkeeper Isaac Collinson has signed his first professional contract with the Blues. Collinson joined Chelsea during his Under-15 season and has developed into a confident and commanding goalkeeper. Last season, Collinson made his Under-18 debut in the Premier League Cup during a 3-3 draw at Cobham. On the international stage, he has previously represented England’s Young Lions at Under-15 and Under-16 level. He has signed the professional deal following his 17th birthday, having signed a scholarship contract back in July 2026.

news.title: Chelsea Women vs Man City: How to watch, kick-off time, live stream info
news.body_en: We are back at Stamford Bridge on Saturday afternoon for a huge fixture against Manchester City in the Women's Super League. This weekend’s match in SW6 is a contest between the top two sides in this season’s Women’s Super League. Chelsea trail Man City by two points with nine games played. London City Lionesses are a further four points behind the Blues. Here is everything you need to know about how to watch Chelsea Women against Man City, including kick-off time and how to follow the action on official Chelsea channels. Chelsea Women's game against Manchester City takes place on Saturday 14 November 2026 at Stamford Bridge, with kick-off scheduled for 1.30pm UK time. The best way to see the game is to join us at the Bridge! Tickets are still available to purchase here. If you can't make the game in person,  then you can watch the action live on BBC One. As always, team news, live updates and match coverage will be provided in our Chelsea Women vs Everton Match Centre on the Chelsea Official App and Chelsea website. You can also follow along via Chelsea Women’s social media channels on X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. The Blues have won seven and drawn two of our nine WSL fixtures so far, with last weekend's 1-1 against Everton ending a seven-game winning streak in the league. We have not failed to win back-to-back top-flight home matches since February/March 2018, when we drew with Manchester City and Reading. Chelsea have had 215 shots in the WSL this season – our average of 24 shots per game is the most by a team in a season in WSL history. Manchester City have won 25 points in their first nine WSL matches this season (W8 D1), their most at this stage of a season since 2017/18 (also 25). As well as the two league meetings last season - one won, one lost - we also played Manchester City in both domestic cup competitions, winning one tie and losing the other. In a League Cup semi-final, a Wieke Kaptein goal secured a 1-0 win away from home. In an FA Cup semi-final at Stamford Bridge, goals from Erin Cuthbert and Sam Kerr were not sufficient to prevent a 3-2 defeat. Manchester City have won just one of their last nine WSL away games against Chelsea (D2 L6), a 1-0 success at Kingsmeadow in February 2024. Chelsea have not lost back-to-back league games against City since a run of four between 2015 and 2017. We suffered our joint-second biggest WSL defeat in our last meeting with Manchester City in February (1-5).

news.title: Chelsea Football Club marks 10 years since historic sexual abuse disclosures in football
news.body_en: November 2026 marks ten years since survivors of childhood sexual abuse began speaking publicly about their experiences in football. Their courage brought to light serious failures in the protection of children and young people and prompted significant change across the game. Chelsea Football Club recognises its own place in this history and acknowledges the harm experienced by those who were failed. We recognise that the impact of abuse can be lifelong and that the experiences of survivors must remain at the centre of how this anniversary is acknowledged. As we mark ten years since these disclosures, we recognise everyone affected by abuse, including those who have not felt able to speak about their experiences. We support the FA's survivor-led Voices of Truth initiative and remain committed to listening to those affected, learning from the past and ensuring that safeguarding remains a priority across the Club. We recognise that this anniversary may be difficult for some people. Anyone affected by abuse who wishes to seek advice, share information or access support can contact the following organisations. If you have experienced or been affected by abuse connected to Chelsea Football Club, whether historic or current, you can contact the Club's Safeguarding Team to discuss your concerns and the support available. Email: safeguarding@chelseafc.com The FA's Voices of Truth platform provides information about the anniversary, relevant independent reviews and support available to those affected by abuse in football. Telephone: 0800 169 1863 (leave a message) NAPAC provides confidential support and information for adults who experienced abuse in childhood. The NSPCC provides advice and support for anyone concerned about the safety or wellbeing of a child. news.title: Late Stamford Bridge winners: vote for your favourite on the Chelsea Official App!
news.body_en: Nothing beats a late winner at Stamford Bridge. The limbs behind the goal. The players racing to one of the corners to celebrate. The banging of the Matthew Harding Stand billboards. There have plenty to enjoy over the years, and now we are asking you to pick your favourite. To help shorten our very lengthy longlist, we have limited our selections to Premier League winners. And they must have been scored in the 85th minute or later. It was incredibly tough for whittle them down to just eight, so we apologise if your favourite didn’t make the final selection! From Lampard to Leboeuf, Estevao to Willian, there are recent and past classics on momentous days in SW6 that will live long in the memory. We start with the quarter-finals today, with the eight goals split into four ties. Watch them back and then vote for your favourite on the Chelsea Official App, with the winners progressing to Saturday’s semis. The grand final will be on Monday! We’ve also added a few lines on each goal for added context if you need help making your mind up! Frank Leboeuf vs Leicester - 1997 Ruud Gullit's Blues had huffed and puffed all game without reward. That was until the ball rolled invitingly into Frank Leboeuf's path, with the centre-back stepping on to it and larruping a spectacular drive into the top corner. William Gallas vs Tottenham - 2006 On the day the King of Stamford Bridge Peter Osgood died, William Gallas conjured up a dramatic late winner from distance at Ossie's beloved Shed End. Claude Makelele vs Charlton - 2005 Claude Makelele chose a memorable moment to score his first Chelsea goal, getting the party started on the day we lifted the Premier League title for the first time with a rebound from his own spot-kick. Estevao Willian vs Liverpool - 2025 We don't think we need to remind you about Estevao's sliding stoppage-time winner against the reigning champions Liverpool last year! Frank Lampard vs Stoke City - 2009 Trailing 1-0, Juliano Belletti drew us level with two minutes to go before Lampard won it in stoppage time with a rising left-footed drive that had the foundations of the Bridge shaking. The Blues were scrapping hard at the top of the table in 2014/15, so it was looking like two points dropped with a goalless draw against Everton. Step forward Willian, whose low striker from a cleared corner find its way into the bottom corner. Fernando Torres vs Man City - 2013 A top-of-the-table clash was settled by Fernando Torres right at the end after a mistake in the Man City backline gave the striker a free run at goal and a tap-in. Cole Palmer vs Man United - 2024 The second-latest winner in Premier League history - after 100 minutes and 41 seconds - was scored by Cole Palmer at the conclusion of a topsy-turvy epic in which our attacker had already equalised deep into stoppage time.

news.title: UEFA Nations League: What the Chelsea players need
news.body_en: The group stage of the UEFA Nations League concludes over the next week, when seven Chelsea players could be in action for their countries with a chance of featuring in the quarter-finals. Spain and defending champions Portugal became the first teams to book their place in the last eight, during the September and October international break. By the end of this window, the rest of the line-up for March's quarter-finals will be completed, ahead of next summer's final tournament. All seven Blues called up by European teams this week have the chance to be there, going into the final two fixtures of the group stage. Here is what they all need to ensure they have a chance to lift the trophy in June. The first group is packed full of Chelsea interest with Malo Gusto, Marco Palestra, Mike Penders and Romeo Lavia all in contention to feature for their countries, representing more than half of the Blues’ seven players called up for Nations League duty in October. Lavia will be suspended when Belgium attempt to repeat last month’s 3-0 win over pointless Turkiye, but will be available to rejoin Penders and Co for what could be a crucial final fixture at home against Italy. Palestra’s Italy sit second, three points behind leaders France and Gusto, one ahead of Belgium. The French's advantage means that even if they lose that first game – and Italy are the only side to deny Les Bleus victory so far – a point against bottom-placed Turkiye would still guarantee them a quarter-final spot, leaving Belgium and Italy to fight it out for the second qualification place. Turkiye vs Belgium, Thursday 12 November, 5pmItaly vs France, Thursday 12 November, 7.45pmFrance vs Turkiye, Sunday 15 November, 7.45pmBelgium vs Italy, Sunday 15 November, 7.45pm Jorrel Hato is not joining the Netherlands squad this month after missing Chelsea’s last three games, although Xabi Alonso is hopeful he will be back at the end of this international break. By then, Hato's international team-mates could have booked their place in the Nations League quarter-finals, going into these games sat at the top of a very tight group. Netherlands vs Greece, Friday 13 November, 7.45pmSerbia vs Germany, Friday 13 November, 7.45pmGermany vs Netherlands, Tuesday 17 November, 7.45pmGreece vs Serbia, Tuesday 17 November, 7.45pm All English eyes will be on veteran captain and this year’s Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane, who is the current Nations League top scorer and will become his country’s all-time appearance maker in his next game. For Chelsea, though, the focus is on fellow attacker Morgan Rogers, Kane’s younger by almost exactly nine years. Spain are already into the quarter-finals and England are on the verge of joining them in second. A point in the Three Lions’ first game against Croatia would seal the deal, avoiding the need to become the first side to take a point off the Spanish. However, with an advantage over third-placed Croatia of six points and a goal difference 21 better, it would take something incredible to deny England a spot in the last eight, regardless. England vs Croatia, Thursday 12 November, 7.45pmCzechia vs Spain, Thursday 12 November, 7.45pmCroatia vs Czechia, Sunday 15 November, 7.45pmSpain vs England, Sunday 15 November, 7.45pm Portugal have already booked their place in the quarter-finals with four wins from as many games so far, and need just a point to guarantee they finish top of their group. That leaves them with little to play for in their games against Denmark and Wales, although they start a new era under coach Jorge Jesus after long-time captain and national hero Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement from international football. Chelsea duo Pedro Neto and Geovany Quenda will both be looking to stake their claim for a place in that new-look attack after being called up for these concluding fixtures to the Nations League group. news.title: Chelsea FC Soccer Schools launches in Australia, bringing our coaching philosophy to thousands of young players
news.body_en: Chelsea FC Soccer Schools is expanding our international programme with the launch of new Soccer Camps in Australia, bringing the club’s renowned coaching methodology and player development approach to young footballers across Melbourne, Sydney and Canberra in January 2027. The camps are a new addition to the growing Chelsea FC Soccer Schools programme, which since 2010 has provided accessible football opportunities for thousands of young people across schools and communities. Designed to inspire a lifelong love of the game, the programmes use the power of football to encourage children and young people to stay active, develop new skills, build confidence and create lasting friendships. At the heart of Chelsea FC Soccer Schools is a commitment to inspiring, educating and engaging the next generation through football. While developing technical ability on the pitch remains a key focus, the programmes are equally dedicated to promoting teamwork, resilience, wellbeing and healthy lifestyles, creating positive experiences that extend far beyond the game itself. Toni Claveria, Director of Football Schools for Chelsea Football Club, said: ‘We are delighted to bring Chelsea FC Soccer Schools to Australia, giving young players the opportunity to experience the club's coaching philosophy while using the power of football to build confidence, create friendships and inspire healthy, active lifestyles. ‘Australia is home to a passionate Chelsea community and, following the visits of both our men's and women's teams during this summer's pre-season tours, we're excited to return so soon. These camps provide a fantastic opportunity to connect with our fans in-country, strengthen our relationship with local communities and inspire the next generation through the game we all love.’ The Australian Soccer Camps will take place over three consecutive weeks in January 2027, giving young players the opportunity to learn directly from official Chelsea FC coaches and experience the club’s coaching philosophy firsthand. Melbourne: 11-15 January at Darebin International Sports Centre Sydney: 18-22 January at North Turramurra Recreation Area Canberra: 25-29 January at David Madew Oval Two programmes will be available at each location. Click to register for the camps. The Development Camp, for boys and girls aged 6-14, will run daily from 8am to 1pm, providing a fun, inclusive and professional environment where players can improve their technical skills, game understanding and confidence. The Performance Camp, for boys and girls aged 15-17, will run from 2.30pm to 5pm and is designed for committed players seeking to further develop their game. Delivered to a smaller, more exclusive group, the programme offers a higher level of individual attention and coaching, supporting talented young players on their football development journey. All camps will be delivered by official Chelsea FC coaches travelling from the UK, ensuring participants experience the same coaching principles and player-centred approach that underpin Chelsea FC Soccer Schools around the world. Five days of coaching delivered by official Chelsea FC coaches An official Chelsea FC Soccer Camps training kit, including t-shirt, shorts and socks Water and fruit throughout the day to support hydration and healthy habits An official Chelsea FC Soccer Camps certificate upon completion The launch forms part of Chelsea FC Soccer Schools' wider ambition to make football accessible to more young people globally, using the game's unique ability to bring communities together, inspire positive change and strengthen connections between the club and its supporters around the world. By expanding into Australia, Chelsea FC Soccer Schools will give young players and families the opportunity to engage directly with the club, while experiencing a programme designed not only to develop footballers but also to encourage confidence, friendship, healthy lifestyles and a lifelong passion for sport. news.title: Four Guinness World Records
Best Jason Cundy celebrations
Chelsea quartet given Guinness World Records titles
news.body_en: Four Chelsea players have been recognised by Guinness World Records for outstanding achievements, with Cole Palmer, Estevao Willian, Hannah Hampton and Manaka Matsukubo each receiving an official certificate. The quartet's records span the men's and women's games, celebrating individual milestones achieved in the Premier League, Brazilian football, the Women's Super League and the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL). All four players are also featured in the Guinness World Records Football Edition 2027, as part of its Class of '27 – a collection of 30 established stars, history-makers and emerging talents. Cole Palmer holds the Guinness World Records title for the fastest perfect hat-trick from kick-off in a Premier League match, having achieved the feat in just 29 minutes against Everton in April 2024. The forward scored with his left foot, right foot and head during the opening half-hour at Stamford Bridge, surpassing the previous record of 38 minutes, which had stood for almost three decades. Palmer went on to complete his hat-trick of hat-tricks – scoring four times in total – as the Blues secured an emphatic 6-0 victory. Estevao’s record was achieved before his move to Stamford Bridge, with the Brazilian becoming the youngest winner of football's Bola de Ouro, aged just 17 years and 229 days. Presented by Brazilian magazine Placar, the award recognises the best player in the country's domestic championship. Estevao received the accolade in December 2024 following an outstanding breakthrough season with Palmeiras, which underlined the exceptional talent that would subsequently bring him to Chelsea. Hannah Hampton is recognised as the youngest goalkeeper to make 100 appearances in the Women's Super League. The England international reached the milestone aged 23 years and 353 days on 3 November 2024, completing her century of WSL outings during Chelsea's 5-0 victory over Everton. Manaka Matsukubo completes the Chelsea quartet after making history in the United States. The Japanese international is the youngest player to score a hat-trick in the National Women's Soccer League, having achieved the feat aged 21 years and 81 days. Matsukubo scored three times for North Carolina Courage against Bay FC on 17 October 2025, setting the record before joining Chelsea in July 2026. Congratulations Cole, Estevao, Hannah and Manaka!

news.title: Internationals: The five key stories to follow
news.body_en: As a number of the Chelsea players head off to join up with their national teams this week, we take a look at the big stories to keep an eye on during this international window. It is a more familiar, shorter, international break in November, following the new extended window introduced last month. There is still plenty going on, though, with several nations rebuilding under new management and Blues in contention to make debuts. Here is what you need to know to follow the key stories involving Chelsea players during this international break… It is impossible for Portugal to avoid the big story in their camp for this window – that they will be without long-serving captain and all-time leading scorer Cristiano Ronaldo, who announced his retirement from international football last week. The two Blues in their squad for November are at very different stages of their own international careers, but will both be looking to play their part in Portugal’s new-look, post-Ronaldo attack. Pedro Neto is one of the experienced, established attackers in the team hoping to fill the gap left by Ronaldo, both in terms of impact on the pitch and leadership. At the other end of the scale is Geovany Quenda, previously a regular for Portugal at youth level, hoping to make his first senior appearance as part of the next generation auditioning to take up the reins. Belgium are another country who will be without one of their experienced regulars, in former Chelsea goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois, who has opted to sit out this Nations League campaign after a series of injuries. That has resulted in a shootout between the other goalkeepers to stake a claim for this tournament and the right to challenge Courtois for the No1 spot on his return. With some strong performances under his belt in the Premier League over the last month, Mike Penders is now hoping to follow up his debut in that competition with another for his national team. Argentina are one of several countries undergoing something of a rebuild after this year’s World Cup, although without a change in management, as Lionel Scaloni looks to inject some youth into his side after the international retirement of Lionel Messi. Among that younger generation looking to impress Scaloni to play an important part in Argentina’s future are 22-year-old Valentin Barco and 21-year-old Aaron Anselmino. Barco already has seven caps to his name, but Anselmino has been called up to the senior squad for the first time. At the other end of the scale is Emiliano Martinez. The goalkeeper is one of Argentina’s most experienced players and a veteran of their 2022 World Cup-winning campaign. After being named on the bench for Chelsea against Sunderland, he could make his return to the pitch following surgery on a fractured jaw during this international window. As well as a crucial couple of games for their Nations League campaign, which could conclude with an effective play-off against Belgium for a place in the quarter-finals, the most important thing for Italy at the moment is to steady the ship after repeated failures to reach the World Cup. That means returning manager Roberto Mancini’s focus is very much on the future. As a result, it is a notably young squad selected for this international window, with only three outfield players over the age of 27. That is a serious departure for a team which has traditionally relied heavily on experience. Among the young contingent is Marco Palestra, returning to the squad following injury for the first time since making his international debut in March. Anselmino isn’t the only Chelsea player meeting up with their national team for the first time in November. After being fast-tracked through the youth ranks in Sweden, Genesis Antwi has been selected by Graham Potter, just one year after making his debut for their Under-21s. Having impressed on loan with Strasbourg so far this season – his first full-time campaign in senior football – Antwi now has his sights set on a senior international debut as Sweden aim to seal promotion to the top tier of the Nations League.

news.title: Bjorn on a good performance just missing a goal
news.body_en: Nathalie Bjorn was pleased with Chelsea’s overall performance and couldn’t fault our effort away at Hacken in the UEFA Women’s Champions League, but gave our opposition credit for the way they defended stubbornly to deny us the winning goal she felt we deserved. The Blues ended Tuesday’s game with a huge 78 per cent share of the possession and managed 20 shots over the 90 minutes. Two of those struck the woodwork and another two found the back of the net, only for both goals to be ruled out by the officials. In the end, despite dominating, Chelsea travelled back to England with just the one point to show for our efforts following a 0-0 draw in Sweden. That was still enough for third place in the table, though, with the Blues undefeated after four games of the league phase and yet to concede a goal in Europe this season. The result left Swedish international defender Bjorn with mixed feelings after having to settle for a point on her return to her homeland. ‘It was a tough game,’ she said. ‘I think we had a good performance but they defended really well. We knew we would have a lot of possession and Hacken are good defensively. ‘We spoke about it, worked on it during the week, but they defended really well. I think we created enough chances to score a goal, but we couldn’t do that this time. We had massive possession, but couldn’t convert the chances. ‘They’re a hard-working team. Swedish teams are known for working really hard defensively and they really proved that. They put bodies on the line, they fought for each other and you could really see the team effort out there. ‘I think we struggled with that. We tried. We really, really tried. But unfortunately we couldn’t score a goal.’ That was despite a notable improvement in the second half, with Bjorn explaining they spent the break discussing the changes needed to improve our chances of victory, even if it wasn’t quite enough in the end. ‘We had a hard time creating some scoring chances, but I think we did, especially in the second half. It was about having more patience in our positions after half-time and I think we did a good performance, but we just couldn't score a goal. ‘We spoke a bit at half-time, to have more players in the box, and I think we did that better in the second half. We had more patience in our possession to see where the spaces were because there were spaces we could play. ‘So I think we played better in the second half, but we just need to be more clinical.’ After back-to-back draws with Everton and Hacken, that need to be more clinical in front of goal is something Bjorn and her Blues team-mates are eager to put right before our next match – a massive top-of-the-table clash in the Women’s Super League against Manchester City at Stamford Bridge. ‘We said we just need to stick together, and we still did a great game. Of course we want to win, we want to have the three points, that was our aim before the game. Sometimes that doesn’t happen, but I think we did a good enough performance to get those three points. ‘It’s just that we couldn’t score the goal, so we just need to take the positives from this game and then bring that in for the game against Manchester City. We just need to sharpen up a little bit and be ready for City this weekend.’ Tickets for Saturday's huge game remain on sale!

news.title: Remembering Vivian Woodward – the amateur and gentleman who sacrificed for others
news.body_en: We continue marking Remembrance Day by celebrating the great Vivian Woodward, who led by example on and off the pitch… When Vivian ‘John’ Woodward died aged 74 in an Ealing nursing home following two years of illness, veteran football writers were quick to acclaim the man who had just slipped the sporting coil. Many described Woodward as one of England’s greatest players, international team-mate Bob Steel recalling ‘the finest centre-forward I have ever seen. A great gentleman on and off the field … I never saw him commit a foul or retaliate – and he took some pastings.’ As a committed amateur with a thriving architectural business, Woodward never claimed a penny from the sport he graced, even the expenses legitimately available to players in his position. That same status enabled him to compete with Great Britain in Olympics – and he won football golds in 1908 and 1912. For the first of those he was a Tottenham squad member, but from November 1909 he was the outstanding star of the recently-formed Chelsea team. ‘The most cheering news we have had during our time of desolation is the intimation that Vivian John Woodward is going to assist Chelsea,’ the Chelsea Chronicle wrote when he signed. ‘Had the great Vivian been a professional player his transfer fee, I fancy, would have been something near a record one. ‘Instead, Woodward comes to us for love, and we may take it that he is already the idol of Stamford Bridge. Vivian Woodward has been and ever will be the people’s favourite. Small wonder. Great as he is as a player, his first claim to popularity lies in the fact that he has ever been first and foremost a gentleman. ‘I question if any footballer has ever been so universally popular, and he carries his honours with the air of a bashful debutant.’ Tall, lithe, his wavy hair slightly receding, the England captain soon became the darling of the Stamford Bridge terracing, netting an impressive 34 goals in 116 appearances for the Blues over six seasons, despite the club’s ups and downs. After the outbreak of World War One in August 1914, like many of his colleagues Woodward answered his country’s call and joined the Army, eventually taking a commission and rising to Captain in the Footballers’ Battalion. Remembrance today means taking a moment to reflect on the personal sacrifice made by so many millions in the face of the unprecedented horrors of 1914-18. To his enormous credit Woodward also made the ultimate act of selflessness in football. On 20 February 1915, then Lieutenant Woodward barked the marching orders to his uniformed men as they paraded the pitch ahead of a round three match between QPR and Everton hosted at Stamford Bridge. Woodward’s participation in football – which carried on as normal for one season – was curtailed by his war service in England (he would not embark overseas until late 1915), and after 29 starts the previous season he was available for just six games, scoring three times, in 1914/15. Significantly, he played no part in the FA Cup campaign as Chelsea roared to the final in April 1915 – the first Football League club from London to do so. Instead, prolific Chelsea-schooled centre-forward Bob Thomson filled his boots in the competition with five goals – including the winner at Man City in round three. Critically, Thomson, who remarkably had the use of only one eye, was sidelined a few weeks after Chelsea beat Everton 2-0 in the semi-final at Villa Park. The final, removed to Old Trafford due to wartime travel restrictions, loomed into view with Thompson working to recover and Woodward suddenly available. Then, as now, the FA Cup showpiece was the dream of any footballer and the opportunity of playing one was all too rare and precious in any career. But when offered the chance to play in place of Thompson, who had barely recovered from his injury, Woodward announced that his fellow striker was the one who had done most to lead Chelsea to the final, and he should be the man to have the honour of representing the Blues on 24 April in Manchester. In the event the so-called ‘Khaki final’ did not go well for David Calderhead’s team – Sheffield United ran out easy 3-0 victors. The player who came to Stamford Bridge ‘for love’ in 1909 was injured in battle and retired from football by the time the Football League returned in 1919, but from 1922 to 1930 he would play another key role as director of the club. Then, until his death a quarter-of-a-century later, Woodward was out of the game – but always remembered for the principled way he approached life and the sport as much as for the brilliance of his stellar career.

news.title: Lucy Bronze: We need to be more ruthless
news.body_en: Lucy Bronze reflected on a frustrating night in Sweden as the Blues were held to a goalless draw by Hacken in the UEFA Women's Champions League, with the defender now turning her attention to this weend’s crucial clash against Manchester City. Sonia Bompastor's side dominated possession and territory throughout, but were unable to break down a resolute Hacken defence. Bronze hit the crossbar in the first half, while both Melvine Malard and Wieke Kaptein had goals ruled out for offside on a night where the Blues created plenty of opportunities without finding the decisive breakthrough. Speaking after the final whistle, Bronze acknowledged that Chelsea needed to show more sharpness in the final third to turn dominance into three points. ‘We probably didn’t do enough in front of the goal to get the ball and to get the win, and Hacken defended really, really well,’ said Bronze. ‘They threw their bodies at the ball all the time. We just needed to be quicker and more slick on the ball, and more ruthless in front of goal, from corners, when we got the chance to take a shot. You need to kill teams when you have so much possession and you dominate the game. ‘Hacken worked really hard. Their game plan worked really well. They were set up to get that point. It is difficult to break a team down, but we can do better than that, and we should be winning games like that.’ With a relentless schedule across domestic and European competitions, the Blues have no time to dwell on Wednesday's result as attention shifts straight back to the Women's Super League. Chelsea host title rivals Manchester City on Saturday, giving Bronze and her team-mates a chance to bounce back immediately in another high-profile fixture. ‘We have a big game coming up in the next couple of days,’ said Bronze. ‘We just recover and we go again like we have all season. news.title: Chelsea Remembers | Remembrance Day
Remembering James Ridley - the Chelsea ballboy who served with Blues greats
news.body_en: This Remembrance Day we tell the story of James Ridley, who served during the First World War and was a well-known figure in the locality of Stamford Bridge for 70 years… Whether it was purchasing his favourite sweet pipe tobacco with a cheery chat at the corner newsagent, or offering his services as a pianist to a women’s group that met in the church, James Ridley always had a tale to tell. When his family caught sight of granddad Jim tinkling the ivories in the church or neighbourhood pub, he seemed transported – eyes glazed, lost in a faraway world. What the listening ladies and evening drinkers might not have known was that Jim had a fascinating life story that of wartime trauma and childhood history-making – all centred around Chelsea Football Club. In 1905, a notice appeared on the gates of the old London Athletic Grounds seeking small boys to fetch the ball when it was hit into the space behind the goals created by the oval athletics track. Chelsea FC were coming to Stamford Bridge and one of the successful young applicants for the new role was Jim, who lived at 7 Stamford Road – opposite the Bridge. He would become one of football’s first ballboys and can be seen on the right of one of the earliest first team photographs, above, taken in September 1905. He had just reached his teens at the time and goalkeeper Willie Foulke – whose stamina the ballboys preserved with their fetching and carrying – would sometimes playfully take him off the field under an arm. Whether he was paid or how much is not known, but the privilege of being at close-quarters to his heroes made Jim a lifelong fan of the club. So much so that in January 1915, a few months after World War One had broken out, Jim – now a 23-year-old labourer a shade over 5ft 5in– volunteered for the recently formed ‘Footballers’ Battalion’ – the 17th Middlesex. He saw it as honour to live, train and fight not just alongside other fans, but many current and former Chelsea players. They included England skipper Vivian ‘Jack’ Woodward, wing-half George Lake, wingers Teddy Foord and Norman Wood, full-back Dave Girdwood, goalkeeper William Krug, legendary all-round sportsman Max Woosnam, and Foulke’s successor at the Bridge, Bob ‘Pom Pom’ Whiting. If you can’t be them, join them seems to have been his maxim, but such commitment came at a price. At the height of the bloody conflict in June 1916, his unit - now part of the 6th Brigade of the 2nd Division of the British Army – found themselves on the frontline, suffering some casualties. The media back home commended the Footballers’ Battalion for their bravery, but the worst was yet to come – including the living hell of the infamous First Battle of the Somme in July 1916, where so many friends were killed or hospitalised. Jim survived, but on 30 November 1917, in the Battle of Cambrai, he was captured by German troops near Inchy. This was where tanks were first truly effective, breaking through the supposedly impregnable Hindenburg Line. Back home, his heartbroken family initially only heard he was ‘missing in action’. Their torment was ended when the Red Cross reported him a prisoner of war at Lager Dulmen. There he would remain until after the war ended by the Armistice at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918. During his 18-month incarceration, guards learned of Jim’s ability on the piano and encouraged him to play one in the camp mess hall as it improved prisoner morale. He was eventually repatriated to Britain on 14 March 1919, returning to civilian life at Stamford Road – and to matches at his beloved Bridge. Playing piano around the area for people’s entertainment was part of the way he dealt with his memories of war. In later life, he would recall what an honour it had been to serve alongside the Chelsea stars – despite the horror of the trenches and darkness of brutal confinement, where forced labour in coal mines was routine. Though always smartly turned-out with a waistcoat and fob-watch, like many ex-soldiers Jim suffered hard times and sadly had to sell his war medals. The ballboy pioneer turned pipe-smoking pianist remained an ardent Blues supporter right up to his death, witnessing the club’s successes in 1955, 1965, 1970 and 1971. Jim died in July 1975, 60 years after joining up to serve King, Country… and Chelsea.

UWCL Highlights: BK Hacken Women 0-0 Chelsea Women
Sonia Bompastor: 'We need to refocus and move on'
news.body_en: Sonia Bompastor felt her side were unfortunate not to come away from Hacken with a win after the Swedish side held us to a stalemate, but stressed the importance of moving on quickly with Saturday's important clash against Manchester City on the horizon. The Blues did everything but score at the Hisingen Arena, hitting the woodwork twice, having two goals ruled out and firing in a total of 32 shots, as Hacken goalkeeper Jennifer Falk was awarded the Player of the Match trophy for making five crucial saves. Defensively, we kept our fourth clean sheet in four league phase matches in the competition, but this was an evening when we were unfortunate not to come away with all three points. Yet there were some positives for the head coach to take, on a night when the defence was solid once again in the Women's Champions League. 'Tonight’s performance was good in terms of the defensive aspects,' Bompastor reflected. 'We knew what they wanted to do against us: they wanted to use the transition to hurt us behind the backline, and the defenders dealt really well with those situations. 'We were dominant with the ball for most of the game. We created a lot of opportunities, but tonight we couldn’t score the one goal to win the game. It’s a frustrating result. We came here with the ambition to win. 'We also hit the crossbar, and the goalkeeper made some great saves. Sometimes it happens in football, and you need to take the learnings and move on. We have enough quality in the squad to achieve that, but tonight it didn’t go our way. 'We have a quick turnaround with a big game at the weekend, so we need to refocus and move on from this one.' Wins over Austria Vienna and Roma plus draws with Lyon and Hacken have seen us take eight points from a possible 12 in the league phase so far. A top-four finish will see us qualify automatically for the knockout stages of the competition, and Bompastor feels that we can't afford to drop any more points. 'I’m quite happy with the way we started the campaign. Tonight was a game where we couldn’t score a goal, but our ambition is still to finish in the top four. We have two games to go in this competition, so we’ll have to win them both and see what happens in the table.'

news.title: UWCL Extended: BK Hacken Women 0-0 Chelsea Women
'We were not clinical and ruthless'
'Hacken put their bodies on the line'
Match report: Hacken 0-0 Chelsea
news.body_en: Chelsea had two goals ruled out and hit the woodwork twice as we battled to a 0-0 draw with Hacken, with the clean sheet preserved thanks to some excellent work from goalkeeper Livia Peng. The match began to the sound of a small but vociferous section of Hacken ultras, who were cheering their side on at the Hisingen Arena in Gothenburg. We kept 73 per cent of the ball during the opening 30 minutes, and despite creating multiple chances, could not convert. There was a feel of deja vu from last Saturday's second half against Everton as we peppered the opposition goal with shots - 21 in total by the 75th minute but still could not steer the ball across the line. But with 691 passes and 32 shots registered by the time the final whistle blew, Chelsea would depart Sweden with just one point in the bag. Sonia Bompastor took full advantage of our squad depth for this midweek trip to Gothenburg, making a total of six changes from the side that drew 1-1 with Everton last Saturday. Hannah Hampton made way for Peng in goal, while Sandy Baltimore, Kadeisha Buchanan, Erin Cuthbert, Katie McCabe and Manaka Matsukubo were replaced in the starting XI by Nathalie Bjorn, Veerle Buurman, Sjoeke Nusken, Lexi Potter and Alyssa Thompson. Our first opportunity came courtesy of Ellie Carpenter's run down the right channel, and her ball into the box was cleared before it could find Thompson in the crowded penalty area. Another cross from Carpenter earned a corner, and Wieke Kaptein had the ball in the back of the net from the resulting set piece, but the goal was ruled out for handball. Up the other end, Hacken broke, and only a superb top-handed save from Peng prevented the home side from taking the lead. It was a frenetic start to the game, and the next opportunity came our way. Buurman strode forward confidently out of defence and played a sideways ball to Kaptein. Quickly switching it to Carpenter, the wing-back advanced on goal but took an extra touch on the ball and ended up shooting into the side netting. We had the ball in the net once more just before the half-hour mark, when Melvine Malard broke through and slotted coolly into the bottom corner, but her attempt was ruled out for offside. Our passing was crisp, and we were creating plenty as we approached the break, and there was yet another close call when a cross-cum-shot from Lucy Bronze bounced off the top of the crossbar. The home side worked diligently to try to extinguish our chances, putting in 11 tackles in the first half alone. Carpenter had served up 10 crosses into the box during the opening 45 minutes, and the second half began with the Australian on the attack again; only a smart stop from former Liverpool goalkeeper Jennifer Falk kept her from putting us ahead. The chances kept coming, and in the 65th minute, Carpenter shot just wide of the right-hand post. And when a fast break saw an Alva Selerud attempt an audacious shot from outside the box, Peng delivered once more with an acrobatic save to push the ball round the post. The Blues managed a break of their own from the resulting corner, and having rounded the goalkeeper, Thompson's run took her just too wide to be able to convert, and her shot was cleared off the line. Substitute Matsukubo was the next player to be unlucky not to score as her close-range effort was saved by Falk. On 86 minutes, Maja Bodin broke through on another quick break. A last-ditch tackle from Buurman and quick reflexes from Peng preserved the clean sheet. As the fourth official indicated six minutes of added time, yet another cross from Carpenter came over into the box and Maika Hamano hit the top of the crossbar with her shot. The Blues couldn't have done much more in attack, but on this occasion, it just wasn't to be. We remain unbeaten and without a single goal conceded in our opening four matches in the UWCL. We move up to second in the league phase standings, pending the rest of the evening's later kick-offs. We return to Stamford Bridge on Saturday for our top-of-the-table Women's Super League clash with Manchester City. Tickets are still available, and you can secure your seat here. news.title: Romeo Lavia: My Football Firsts

The in-form midfielder recalls life growing up in Belgium, and remembers how it felt to sign for the Blues back in 2023… What was the first game you attended? Anderlecht against Standard Liege. A big game, the biggest in Belgium. It was a top atmosphere. I must have been seven or eight. It was pretty cool. What was the first kit you owned? I think it was a Brazil shirt with Ronaldo on the back and number nine. Who was the first team you played for? My grassroots team was called Woluwe-Zaventem. She was called Natalie. She gave me the opportunity to move to an elite club, Anderlecht. Who was your first friend in football? His name is Hugo Masaki. He plays for UD Leiria in Portugal now. Who was the first team-mate you roomed with on an away trip? Who was your first team debut against? My first-team debut was with Man City against Wycombe Wanderers. What was the first goal you scored? That was for Southampton against Chelsea. I’m happy I have scored one for Chelsea now! When was the first time you were recognised in public? I must have been 15, when I was still at Anderlecht. It was in Brussels, and it was a very strange feeling! They must have been a big fan to know who I was. What was your first emotion after signing for Chelsea? Very proud, yeah. And I had all my family around, which made me even more grateful, happy, and excited.

news.title: Nathalie Bjorn on why facing Hacken will be 'no walk in the park'
news.body_en: Nathalie Bjorn is back in her native Sweden this week as we take on Hacken in the Women’s Champions League, with the defender hitting form at the perfect moment. Leaving behind last season’s injury battle, Bjorn enjoyed her first start for the Blues this season in the 6-0 WSL win over Charlton, leading the side out as captain. The day couldn’t have gone much better for Bjorn as she opened the scoring with a header after just three minutes at The Valley. As she explains when she sits down to talk to us ahead of the trip to Sweden, she’s feeling excited for the rest of the campaign. ‘It’s been good,’ Bjorn says. ‘I’m taking it day by day, and I’m very happy that my body is feeling good. 'It’s difficult coming back from a long-term injury, in terms of having the quality on the pitch and getting back to my old self. I know it will take time, so I’m trying to be open-minded and grateful that my body is doing what I want it to do. ‘I want to push my standards even higher, and I feel like I still have a few steps to go before I’m back to my prior self. But the season has been good. The team has been amazing and performed really well, and I think this is a very exciting season for us. ‘It was a really nice feeling to walk out with the armband and have the girls with me,' adds Nat. 'A proud moment for me, and obviously even better to score the goal. It was my first start in almost a year at Chelsea, which made it a really nice feeling. ‘We had loads of different goalscorers, and players who haven’t played as much this season got the chance to prove themselves. The game really showed the quality we have in the squad this year.’ Talking with Bjorn is an ideal opportunity for us to glean some insight into Tuesday night’s opponents and the wider Swedish league. From what she describes, the Blues supporters can expect a fascinating evening in Gothenburg. ‘Hacken are a good team,’ she explains. ‘Some of them are my team-mates in the national team. I played with their head coach before, and I know she’s a very good, very passionate coach. I played with their captain Anna Anvegard at Everton. I know them really well. ‘They are a hard-working side, and they’ve done well in Europe in previous seasons, so it’s not going to be a walk in the park for us. They also have a big supporter group at their home games, so I think it’s going to be an amazing atmosphere. I’m looking forward to it. ‘A few years back, the Swedish league was one of the biggest leagues in the world, with players such as Marta da Silva, Lotta Schelin and Christen Press,’ she tells us. 'There are loads of good Swedish players, too. ‘The number of players coming from the Swedish league to the English league proves that the quality there is really good. I took the step from the Swedish league to England myself. It’s a good league for preparing players to go out and play in Europe.' Bjorn moved to the Women’s Super League when she joined Everton back in 2021. We ask her about the difference between life in Scandinavia and England, and what she misses about home. ‘England is quite similar in a way, which is really nice,’ she smiles. ‘It feels like a home away from home. It’s easy to adapt to. Of course, there are different traditions and different types of food – I would say that’s maybe the biggest difference. ‘When I first came to England, it was an easy transition because we learn English in school. So with that and the culture being quite similar, it makes it really easy. ‘I miss the Swedish food. I miss Swedish pick and mix! Every time my parents or my siblings come over, I always ask them to bring some. I really miss Swedish cheese. We eat breakfast with hard bread and butter, and then we slice the cheese up. ‘But here we don’t have exactly the same assortment, or you buy slices already cut, and they’re quite thick, but I like them a bit thinner. It goes in phases, but right now, I miss the cheese and also liquorice!’ Bjorn will have a brief moment to sample those home comforts before focus turns to business. Today's task is returning to London with three more Champions League points.

news.title: UNCUT TRAINING ahead of Hacken 💫
Bompastor on latest team news and needing to be at our best against Hacken
news.body_en: Sonia Bompastor feels that Tuesday night's UEFA Women's Champions League fixture against Hacken has come at exactly the right time to help Chelsea shake off Saturday's disappointing 1-1 draw with Everton in domestic action. The stalemate with the Toffees saw Sandy Baltimore put us in front with a header, but an unfortunate own goal from Lucy Bronze levelled the scores. And despite our best efforts in the second half, we couldn't put ourselves back in front. There's little time between Saturday afternoon's final whistle and Tuesday's 5.45pm kick-off (UK time) in Gothenburg, but Bompastor feels that it will be good to get back out on the pitch quickly to shake off the result against Everton. And aside from Naomi Girma and Lauren James, who were not part of the travelling squad, the head coach confirmed she has a full complement to pick from. 'All the other players are fit and available,' said Bompastor, before going on to discuss our impressive record in the Champions League, in which we have not conceded a single goal in our opening three league phase encounters. 'It’s important for us to stay in that good form, especially on the back of a disappointing result at the weekend. 'In this competition we also have ambitions, and right now we are in the top four. That’s the goal: we want to be in the top four and stay there. So we want to put in a good performance and get a good result tomorrow. Staying strong defensively, not conceding too much and keeping a clean sheet would be a good thing.' In a match where we had 65 per cent possession and fired 20 shots towards goal against Everton, the head coach said she was frustrated not to take all three points. But football moves on quickly, and Bompastor wants to take the opportunity to put in an improved display against Hacken. 'I think the frustration came from the result because we have ambitions, and dropping two points at home is never good, but it happens. The good thing with a quick turnaround is you analyse the game and give the players feedback, but you also need to move on. You need to focus on something new. We have a new game coming, in a new competition, so it’s the best thing for us in terms of moving on.' Hacken were crowned Swedish champions for the second year running last week, and won the inaugural Women’s Europa Cup last season. However, their Champions League campaign has been tougher, with defeats to Inter and Juventus followed by a 1-1 draw away at Paris FC, secured by a 93rd-minute equaliser. Bompastor believes those results haven’t reflected Hacken’s performances, and she warned of the threats they carry. 'Hacken's Champions League results didn’t necessarily reflect their performances on the pitch,' Bompastor explained. 'They have strengths and threats, especially in the attacking line, with speed and pace. So we will have to be really careful in the transitional moments of the game. 'For me, it’s important we find the right balance between focusing on ourselves and making sure we don’t give them many opportunities. They are playing at home, so they’ll want a good result, and we need to be at our best tomorrow.'

news.title: Chelsea Women travelling squad confirmed for Hacken
news.body_en: A 23-player Chelsea squad has been confirmed for the Women's Champions League match away at Hacken.
